messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus Vance still recalls the morning in 1987 when the Coast Guard supply vessel Marianne ruptured a pressurized drum of industrial solvent off the Jersey coast. At twenty-four, he stood on the dew-slicked deck when the valve blew, releasing a thick, acrid vapor that clung to the metal grating and burned his throat. There was no time to reach his half-mask. The deck fell into a stunned hush as crewmen scrambled for respirators, and Marcus felt the sudden, suffocating weight of the chemical cloud settling into his lungs. The incident did not end when they secured the spill; it anchored itself in his nervous system. Over the decades, he had come to believe that unusual silence made him feel something dangerous was about to happen, a conviction born on that quieted deck where the only warning was the absence of sound. The memories refused to stay contained. What frightened him most was that his memories of the frightening event were like a film that played over and over, each frame as sharp and unyielding as a photograph. When the recall returned, he would feel so overwhelmed by emotion that he had to stop whatever he was doing, gripping the edge of his kitchen counter until his shoulders shook. Those vivid intrusions did not merely frighten him; they recalibrated his expectations of his own capacity and the world around him. He had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place, that he could not deal with even the slightest upset, and that if he thought about the event, he would not be able to handle it. The memories, in turn, kept pulling his body back into the simulation of the spill. As soon as the film would begin, his physical reactivity would spike: his chest would tighten, his palms would sweat, and his breath would shorten into shallow, desperate hitches that felt exactly like the chemical burn of 1987. At his waterfront home, the cycle tightened with predictable cruelty. Because he was certain he could not cope with even the slightest upset, he scanned every room for signs of instability, treating the stillness of his living room like a held breath waiting to break. When that vigilance caused his pulse to climb and his muscles to lock, the physical reactivity fed directly into his convictions, confirming his fear that the world was dangerous and his own fragility was absolute. The dread of the quiet, in turn, became a trigger that almost immediately summoned the photographic recall, pulling him back into the yellow haze of the deck. Marcus had built a daily routine around what he was running from: he checked the carbon monoxide detector three times a day, kept the windows cracked just a finger’s width, and avoided driving near industrial ports where the air carried that familiar solvent tang. Even after forty years in the Coast Guard, his wife Elena noticed how his posture stiffened the moment the house went quiet, how his eyes darted to the doorframe as if watching for a leak that wasn’t there. What finally brought him to the clinic was a night he spent pacing the hardwood floor, convinced the silence was a prelude to disaster, until he realized he could no longer hold the line. He was afraid that without help, the loop would keep teaching him to fear the quiet, but he hoped, against the weight of years, that someone might help him untangle the thread before the past pulled him under completely.
